notes.definition: Metals have giant structures of atoms (positive ions) held together by strong metallic bonding, so most have high melting and boiling points. Alloys are mixtures of a metal with other elements, usually other metals; they are harder than pure metals because the different-sized atoms distort the layers.
explanation: Metals consist of giant structures in which positive metal ions are arranged in a regular pattern, surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons. Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. This bonding acts throughout the whole structure and is strong, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. This means that most metals have high melting and boiling points. For example, iron melts at 1538 °C. (A few metals, such as mercury, which is liquid at room temperature, are exceptions.)

In a pure metal, all the atoms are the same size and are arranged in regular layers. When a force is applied, the layers can slide over each other. The metallic bonding is not broken when this happens, because the delocalised electrons can move with the ions and keep holding the structure together. This is why pure metals can be bent, hammered and shaped (they are malleable and ductile) rather than shattering.

Because their layers slide so easily, many pure metals are too soft for everyday uses. Pure gold, pure copper and pure iron, for example, bend and wear away too easily. To make them harder, metals are mixed with other elements, usually other metals, to make alloys. Steel, for example, is an alloy of iron with small amounts of carbon and sometimes other metals.

Alloys are harder than pure metals because the atoms of the added element are a different size from the atoms of the main metal. The different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers are no longer flat and lined up. This makes it much more difficult for the layers to slide over each other. More force is needed to change the shape of an alloy, so it is harder and stronger than the pure metal.

An alloy is a mixture, not a compound, so its composition can be varied. Chemists can change the amounts of the elements to make alloys with the properties needed for a particular use, such as hardness, strength or resistance to corrosion. In exam questions you may be given the percentage composition of an alloy and asked to calculate the mass of each element in a sample.
keyFacts: Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding.
Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Most metals have high melting and boiling points because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the metallic bonding.
In pure metals the atoms are all the same size and arranged in layers.
The layers can slide over each other, so pure metals can be bent and shaped.
Pure metals are often too soft for many uses.
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, usually other metals.
Alloys are harder because different-sized atoms distort the layers, making it more difficult for them to slide.

keyTerms.definition: The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and the shared sea of delocalised electrons.
Outer electrons that are not tied to any one atom and are free to move through the whole metal structure.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals, made to improve the metal's properties.
Able to be hammered or bent into shape without breaking.
The regular rows of identical atoms in a pure metal, which can slide over each other.
Disruption of the regular layers in an alloy caused by atoms of a different size.

equations.name: Percentage by mass of an element in an alloy
equations.formula: percentage of element = (mass of element ÷ total mass of alloy) × 100

workedExamples.title: Mass of a metal in an alloy
workedExamples.question: A brass ornament has a mass of 250 g. The brass is 70% copper and 30% zinc by mass. Calculate the mass of copper in the ornament.
steps: Write the percentage as a decimal: 70% = 0.70.

workedExamples.title: Percentage composition of an alloy
workedExamples.question: A 40 g sample of an alloy contains 36 g of tin and 4 g of copper. Calculate the percentage of tin by mass.

workedExamples.title: Explaining hardness
workedExamples.question: Explain why steel is harder than pure iron.
steps: Pure iron: all atoms the same size, arranged in regular layers that slide easily.
Steel: contains atoms of other elements (such as carbon) of a different size.
So the layers cannot slide over each other as easily, and more force is needed to change the shape.
workedExamples.answer: The different-sized atoms in steel distort the layers of iron atoms, making it more difficult for the layers to slide over each other, so steel is harder.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that alloys are harder because the bonds in alloys are stronger.
misconceptions.right: In fact the explanation is about structure: different-sized atoms distort the layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that when a metal is bent, the metallic bonds are broken.
misconceptions.right: In fact the layers slide over each other but the delocalised electrons move with them, so the metallic bonding still holds the structure together.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an alloy is a compound of two metals.
misconceptions.right: In fact an alloy is a mixture. Its composition can be varied, and the elements are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals have high melting points because of strong covalent bonds or strong intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.right: In fact metals have strong metallic bonding: the electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons throughout a giant structure.

realWorld: Steel (iron with carbon) is used for bridges, buildings and car bodies because it is much harder and stronger than pure iron.
Gold used in jewellery is usually alloyed with copper or silver because pure gold is too soft and would scratch and bend.
Copper is used for water pipes because it can be easily bent and shaped, which depends on the layers of atoms sliding over each other.
examTips: For 'explain why alloys are harder', the marks are for: different-sized atoms, distort the layers, layers cannot slide (as easily). Use all three ideas.
Do not write that alloys have 'stronger bonds'; it is the distortion of the layers that matters.
When explaining high melting points of metals, name the attraction: between positive ions and delocalised electrons, and say it is strong so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it.
In percentage calculations, check that your answers add up to the total mass of the alloy.
summary: Metals have giant structures with strong metallic bonding.
Most metals have high melting and boiling points.
Atoms in pure metals are in layers that slide, so metals can be bent and shaped.
Pure metals are often too soft for use.
Alloys are mixtures of a metal with other elements, usually metals.
Different-sized atoms distort the layers in an alloy, so it is harder.

options: The bonds in an alloy are stronger than in a pure metal
An alloy contains more delocalised electrons
Different-sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide over each other as easily
The atoms in an alloy are all the same size, so they pack more tightly
markScheme: 1 mark: Different-sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide over each other as easily
questions.explanation: Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers. Distorted layers do not slide easily, so the alloy is harder. It is not about stronger bonds.

questions.question: What happens to the metallic bonding when a piece of copper wire is bent?
options: The metallic bonds all break
The layers slide but the metallic bonding still holds the structure together
The copper atoms become ions for the first time
The delocalised electrons are lost from the metal
markScheme: 1 mark: The layers slide but the metallic bonding still holds the structure together
questions.explanation: As the layers slide, the delocalised electrons move with the ions, so the attraction between ions and electrons is maintained.

questions.question: Metallic bonding is the attraction between which particles?
options: Positive metal ions and negative ions
Neighbouring metal atoms sharing a single pair of electrons
Protons in the nucleus and electrons in inner shells
Positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: Positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the lattice of positive ions and the delocalised electrons around them.

questions.question: Steel is an alloy containing iron and carbon. In which way is steel different from pure iron?
options: Steel is softer
Steel is harder
Steel has a regular arrangement of identical atoms
Steel does not contain metallic bonding
markScheme: 1 mark: Steel is harder
questions.explanation: The carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms and distort the layers, so steel is harder than pure iron. Steel still has metallic bonding.

questions.explanation: A pure metal contains only one type of atom, so A, with rows of identical atoms in regular layers, is the pure metal. B has atoms of two different sizes (an alloy), C shows separate small molecules and D shows alternating positive and negative ions (an ionic compound).

questions.question: Name the type of bonding in metals.
markScheme: 1 mark: metallic (bonding)
questions.explanation: Metals are held together by metallic bonding between positive ions and delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Give one reason why gold used for jewellery is usually an alloy, not pure gold.
acceptedAnswers: less likely to bend or scratch
markScheme: 1 mark: pure gold is too soft / the alloy is harder so it does not bend or scratch as easily
questions.explanation: Pure gold's layers slide easily, so it is soft; alloying makes it harder and more durable.

questions.question: Explain why most metals have high melting points.
acceptedAnswers: strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: giant structure with strong metallic bonding / strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
1 mark: a lot of energy is needed to overcome this bonding
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed: what the bonding is and why it leads to a high melting point (lots of energy needed).

markScheme: 1 mark: alloy contains atoms of different sizes
1 mark: these distort the (regular) layers
1 mark: so it is more difficult for the layers to slide over each other
questions.explanation: Three linked ideas: different sizes, distortion, harder to slide. Saying 'the bonds are stronger' gains no credit.

questions.question: A sample of pure aluminium is soft. Suggest how a manufacturer could make a harder material from aluminium and explain why it would be harder.
markScheme: 1 mark: mix the aluminium with another metal / element to form an alloy
1 mark: different-sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide easily
questions.explanation: Alloying is the standard way to harden a metal; the explanation is distortion of layers.

questions.question: Explain why metals can be bent without breaking, whereas ionic compounds such as sodium chloride shatter when hit.
acceptedAnswers: ionic: like charges line up and repel
markScheme: 1 mark: in metals the layers slide and the delocalised electrons keep the positive ions held together (bonding maintained)
1 mark: in ionic compounds moving a layer brings ions with the same charge next to each other, so they repel and the crystal breaks
questions.explanation: The delocalised electrons in a metal move with the ions so the structure holds together; in an ionic lattice a shift lines up like charges, which repel.

questions.question: A metal Z has a melting point of 1085 °C. When it is alloyed with a small amount of a second metal, the alloy is much harder. A student says this is because the bonds in the alloy are stronger. Evaluate the student's statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: the student is incorrect (hardness is not mainly due to stronger bonds)
1 mark: the different-sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide over each other as easily
questions.explanation: The correct explanation for hardness in alloys is structural, based on distortion of the layers.

questions.question:

markScheme: 1 mark: 60 g
questions.explanation: 60% of 100 g is 60 g.

questions.question:

The brass is 65% copper by mass.
Calculate the mass of copper in the key.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 26 g
questions.explanation: 65 ÷ 100 × 40 = 26 g. Check: the zinc would be 14 g, and 26 + 14 = 40 g.

markScheme: 1 mark: = 82%

questions.question:

1 tonne = 1000 kg
markScheme: 1 mark: 1.2 tonnes = 1200 kg
questions.explanation: Convert to kilograms first: 1200 kg. 0.25% of 1200 kg = 0.0025 × 1200 = 3 kg. A common error is to use 0.25 as a decimal (giving 300 kg).

questions.question:
Solder is an alloy of tin and lead.
Table 1 shows information about a reel of solder.
The rest of the solder is lead.
Calculate the percentage by mass of lead in the solder.
markScheme: 1 mark: mass of lead = 250 − 150 = 100 g
questions.explanation: First find the mass of lead (100 g), then divide by the total mass: 100 ÷ 250 × 100 = 40%. Giving the tin percentage (60%) is a common slip.

markScheme: Indicative content: iron is a metal with a giant structure; atoms arranged in regular layers; all atoms the same size; layers can slide over each other easily; so pure iron is soft and bends easily. Steel contains carbon atoms, which are a different size from iron atoms; these distort the layers; layers cannot slide as easily; so steel is harder and stronger; a bridge must not bend or change shape under load; so steel is more suitable.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of the two structures with a logical explanation of hardness, linked to the use in bridges.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'steel is harder' or 'iron has layers', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Top answers contrast the regular layers in iron with the distorted layers in steel and link this to steel being harder and not bending under load.

questions.question:
Copper is used to make electrical wires and water pipes. For coins, copper is mixed with nickel to make an alloy.
Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why copper has a high melting point and can be shaped into wires and pipes, and why an alloy is more suitable than pure copper for making coins.
markScheme: Indicative content: copper has a giant metallic structure; positive copper ions in regular layers; surrounded by delocalised electrons; strong electrostatic attraction between ions and delocalised electrons (metallic bonding); lots of energy needed to overcome the bonding so high melting point. Atoms are all the same size, in layers; layers slide over each other when a force is applied; metallic bonding is maintained as electrons move with ions; so copper can be bent, drawn into wires and shaped into pipes. Pure copper is too soft for coins; coins would bend and wear away; nickel atoms are a different size; they distort the layers; layers cannot slide over each other as easily; alloy is harder; coins keep their shape and resist wear.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, coherent explanation covering metallic bonding and high melting point, sliding layers and shaping, and distortion of layers making the alloy harder, linked to the uses.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains two of the three areas clearly, or all three with some gaps in reasoning.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple, relevant statements with little or no explanation.
questions.explanation: The question needs three linked explanations: strong metallic bonding (high melting point), sliding layers (shaping) and distorted layers (harder alloy for coins).

questions.question: State one property of most metals that is explained by strong metallic bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark: high melting point / high boiling point
questions.explanation: Strong metallic bonding needs a lot of energy to overcome, giving high melting and boiling points.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of two metals.
Use the information in Table 1 to evaluate the statement:
'All metals have high melting points.'
acceptedAnswers: most metals have high melting points
markScheme: 1 mark: most metals have high melting points (for example iron) because of strong metallic bonding
1 mark: but the statement is not true for all metals, as mercury is liquid at room temperature (so has a low melting point)
questions.explanation: AQA states that 'most' metals have high melting points. Mercury shows the generalisation has exceptions.
